comments.author: UnderLord7985
comments.body:
Yeah you should have a GDD or some sort of pathway for it to follow, then from there you can add in more as needed, if explained correctly the AI can do it with little effort and usually be 95% correctly done. 

But for other things it might forget something or add in stuff you didnt want so after each iteration you need to play test to make sure its correct or it can get out of hand quickly. 

For me i do one simple iteration to get the process started, for instance i had the AI pool all the information about the game into a help document which can be accessed inside the game to help explain things. 

It did this well, now the next step is to look at the entire document and see where it can be clearer / easier to read. 

The AI likes to short hand stuff or leave out words that would otherwise switch the meaningo of something. So you also gotta proof read, so it'll end up just being me, reading and editing it manually, which is fine.

comments.author: meowyih
comments.body: You are the one who should design the "good architecture", not AI. You have to create the architecture module by module with AI assistants. Each module should be loose coupling and independent. So something bad happen, you can rewrite and replace only a  small part of the whole project. AI is bad at that, it's your responsibility. But on the other hand, if you don't care the maintenance or reusability, when something bad happen, just start another project and rewrite everything, then you don't have to waste your time on it. :>

comments.author: geldonyetich
comments.body:
Depends. Cheap Chinese models aren't necessarily terrible. My experiences with Qwen 3.8-27b and Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is it's pretty great. I'm not talking frontier level performance, but far better than you might expect for something you can run on local inference.

Check out [some coding benchmarks](https://www.ai-leaderboard.dev/) before you choose a model, prioritize SWE-bench results. If you're hosting your own, it's best to code with a quant precision above IQ4, some MoE are a little more robust than that but I still think it's a good rule of thumb.

As for enforcing good architecture, honestly to an extent that's going to be up to you. If you don't get in there often to touch up the code yourself, of course the arch is going to drift a bit from your concept of "good" because it's going to stop being your arch.

comments.author: Toastti
comments.body:
This is the moment you should really sit down and learn best coding practices for the language you use along with best Git practices. 

And I mean actually learn. Don't let the AI code a single line for you. You type it and can ask AI to teach you, explain what's next, how to use this function, how to inherit classes, how to properly declare types etc. 

Even if you don't end up writing a single manual line after learning this. You can still use everything you learned to prompt AI properly. What classes own what gameplay element. How to store all modifiable attributes as a Json config file to tweak yourself to decide what feels fun in your game, etc. 

You can't expect to make an amazing and fun game without putting some human touches. AI is incredibly smart, but it honestly doesn't know what 'fun' means. That is for you to decide and instruct the AI about.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
By not leaving architecture to AI, plain and simply. Different models only differ marginally here.

Once the architecture of your codebase has matured and stabilised, and you are mostly adding things in already established patterns, you can be less concerned with the code and architecture.

But whenever you add a new concept to your codebase, you need to make some decisions.

In other words: Learn software engineering. AI can help you with that. You probably don't even need to study it for years and get a degree in it. The problem is the vibe coder attitude of "I don't need to learn anything".

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
I should add that "bad" architectute produced by AI is most of the time not an issue of AI being had at architecture, and it is definitely not a model problem.

It's because **your AI cannot know what your long term vision is unless you tell it**.

If you ask AI to build the first slice of your game or whatever, it will build only what is needed to make that work. Then you have a prototype that you may be unable to shape into something bigger.

Unless you are building a custom engine, architecture isn't actually that important. Godot, UE, or whatever should already be giving you a solid framework. Note that three.js is not a game engine, so if you build on three.js, you are effectively building your own custom engine.

In short, slow the f... down, think, improve your SWE skills.
